headline: Southwest Ledge Turns Warm and Green — Bass Holding Deep While Block Island Waits on Bonito
subhead: The water off the island is warming fast, pushing stripers into deeper structure while the first bonito push sits right on the edge of showing.
body_markdown:
_AI fishing-intelligence report. It was prepared from 0 supplied evidence records and 17 supplied analysis inputs; it does not claim firsthand fishing._

There's a change you feel before you can name it — the swells off the Southwest Ledge have gone from cobalt to a warm, hazy green, and that green water tells you more than any thermometer. It means the surface layer has thickened up, the bait's pushed shallow, and the stripers that made this island famous have started sliding off the top and hugging the cooler seams down deep. That's the story of the week here: good fish, but you have to go get them.

The regional numbers back up what the water's showing. New London is reading 77.4°F, Kings Point 74.8°F, and the open ocean off the Bight is sitting at 75.9°F with a 3.6-foot swell running on a 6-second period — enough chop to make positioning over structure a real job on an outboard, but nothing that shuts the bite down if you pick your window. Striped bass are cold-water fish at heart, and when the surrounding water climbs into the mid-to-high 70s, they don't leave — they go down. The North Rip and the deeper humps off the Southwest Ledge, where the current stacks bait against structure in 40 to 60 feet, are holding the better class of fish right now. Reports out of that zone describe bass working the bottom third of the water column on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, when the rip stands up hardest and sand eels get pinned against the ledge. Diamond jigs and 2-ounce bucktails dressed with a white or chartreuse Fin-S trailer, worked with a slow lift-and-drop right on bottom, are the play. Don't be in a hurry to work them back up — the bite's been coming on the fall, not the retrieve.

Fluke are still cooperating on the sand-bottom flats off the south side, particularly in that stretch running toward the Great Salt Pond entrance where the bottom transitions from mud to clean sand in 25 to 35 feet. Drifting the incoming tide with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet, or a straight bucktail-and-squid-strip combo, has been the more consistent producer than bait alone this week — the current's been strong enough that a heavier jig head holds bottom contact better than a spinner rig. Sizes have been mixed, plenty of shorts mixed with keeper-class fish to four and five pounds, so it pays to cover ground rather than anchor on one drift.

Bluefish have been the most reliable violence on the water. Wherever the bunker schools have bunched up tight — and there's been no shortage of bunker pushing along the island's west side this month — the blues have been all over them on top, and it's been about as advertised. We flagged this pattern last week, that as long as high pressure holds and bunker stay concentrated, the topwater blitzes would keep coming, and that's exactly what's playing out. Poppers and metal-lip swimmers thrown right into the boil, worked fast, have been drawing violent strikes, mostly cocktail-to-medium blues in the 4 to 8-pound range with the occasional bigger fish mixed in.

Scup are thick around the rock piles and mussel beds ringing the island — Southwest Ledge, the breakwaters off New Harbor, the structure off Sandy Point — and squid have been showing in good numbers as well, which is exactly the kind of bait buildup that tends to precede the first bonito of the season. That's the piece everyone's watching for. We noted a few days back that water temps at Montauk, Block Island, and the Buzzards Bay corridor were closing in on the threshold that typically triggers the first bonito run, and the numbers coming in now — Montauk at 74.5°F, the open Bight near 76°F — put this window right in that band. Nothing confirmed yet on the island's south side, but the ingredients are lined up: warming surface water, dense bait, and settled high pressure. If it's coming, it'll show first on the rips off the Southeast Light or around the Cinder Block, small fast-moving epoxy jigs and Deadly Dix worked on light spin gear the standard approach once the schools materialize.

Blackfish season is still off in the distance, but the structure that'll hold them later — the rock piles off the north end and the Ledge itself — is already thick with the crab and mussel forage that makes those spots productive come fall.

Looking ahead, the pattern favors patience over urgency. If the high pressure holds and surface temps keep their slow climb, expect the bonito question to get answered within the next week to ten days, and when it does, the south side rips will be the first place to look. Until then, the smart money stays on working the North Rip and Southwest Ledge on the tide changes, fishing bass deep and bluefish on the surface wherever the bunker show. It's not a blowout week, but it's an honest one — the fish are here, they're just asking you to go find them instead of waiting for them to come to you.
